chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from al-Qasim ibn 'Urwah, from Zurarah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The divorced woman may apply kohl, dye (her hair), perfume herself, and wear whatever clothes she wishes.
Because Allah, the Exalted, says: 'Perhaps Allah will bring about after that some new matter (of reconciliation).'

key_terms.الْمُطَلَّقَةُ: A woman who has been given a revocable divorce (talaq raj'i) and is in her waiting period (iddah).
key_terms.تَخْضَبُ: She dyes (typically referring to henna for hands/hair).
key_terms.لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ: Perhaps Allah will bring about (indicating the possibility of a new event, i.e., reconciliation).

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for a divorced woman's attire and behavior during the waiting period in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In al-Istibsar, Shaykh al-Tusi cites this chain from Zurarah to Imam al-Sadiq to clarify that the 'waiting period' (iddah) for a revocable divorce (talaq raj'i) does not entail seclusion (hidad) or restriction on adornment, distinguishing it from the widow's iddah. The ruling is grounded in the Quranic phrase 'Perhaps Allah will bring about after that a new situation' (65:1), which implies the husband's active possibility of remarriage (ruju') during this time, thus permitting the wife to remain in her normal state of beauty and readiness for potential reconciliation.
